title: Navigation for a two-sided marketplace
metaTitle: Marketplace navigation as a job map
excerpt: Navigation should list jobs the scarce side already has words for, with one path that joins that side. Department names force a translation nobody came to do.
alt: A white wall covered with framed prints, small plants, and two floating shelves, a grid of choices that still needs labels a visitor can use.
caption: Framed prints and small plants arranged on a white wall. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many items belong in a marketplace header?
faqs.answer: Five to seven items is enough for a phone, if each one is a job. Include a join path for the scarce side, a way to see the fee, and a way to see a real example. Move departmental pages and one-off campaigns to the footer or cut them. Nested menus hide the action that seeds the market.

faqs.question: Should both sides get equal emphasis in the menu?
faqs.answer: Both sides need a door. They do not need the same visual weight. Style the scarce side's join path as the action, and keep the other side's item as a plain link with their own words. Equal buttons in the header repeat a homepage problem on every page of the site.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Sign in and Join?
faqs.answer: Sign in is for someone who already has an account. Join, apply, or list is for someone who does not. Sending a new applicant into a password field makes the market feel closed. Keep one label for the join path in the header, the footer, and the buttons, and send that label to the same short form.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The two-sided marketplace website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of departments. The side you need first should see labels they already use, and one of those paths should join that side. Everything else is a way to get back.

If the menu reads like the inside of the company, a stranger has to translate before they can act. They will not. They will use the one control that looks like a button, even when it is the wrong door.

## Jobs, not departments

Write the jobs on a card before you open the header. For a kitchen market that needs hosts: list a dinner, see the fee, read how a night runs, apply. For a freight board that needs carriers: post capacity, see a rate, read the rules, join. Those are navigation items. "Company," "Platform," "Resources," and "Solutions" are folders.

The W3C's WCAG overview organizes accessibility into four principles: content should be perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation is where operable and understandable meet. People need to reach the jobs from a keyboard and from a phone, and the labels need to mean the same thing every time they appear. A menu that only makes sense after a hover, or that renames the same job on every page, fails both principles in ordinary language.

Put the join path in the header as a real item, with the same words as the homepage button. "Apply as a host" should not become "Get started" in the corner and "Partner with us" in the footer. Three names for one door look like three products.

Limit the header. Five to seven items is a range you can defend on a phone. If you have more jobs than that, the extras belong in a footer grouped by side, or on the services page, not in a mega-menu copied from a company with a hundred products.

## Words they already use

Collect the words from support mail, from application forms, and from the way the scarce side describes the work to each other. Use those words as labels. "Shifts" or "visits" or "loads," not a coined product name, unless the coined name is truly what they type.

Test the labels without the design around them. Read the list to someone from that side. Ask where they would click to join, where they would click to understand the fee, and where they would click if a job went wrong. If they hesitate, the label is clever or internal. Change the label, not the person's vocabulary.

The other side gets labels too, and they should not be forced through a translator. "Book a seat" and "Host a dinner" can both live in the menu if the weight is not equal. The join path for the scarce side is the item you style as the action. The other side's item can be a plain link. Equal styling in the header repeats the homepage mistake one level up, where it is visible on every page.

Avoid "for teams / for individuals" unless those are the words they use. Many markets are not teams and individuals. They are clinics and clinicians, shippers and carriers, families and sitters. Use the pair you actually serve.

## One path that joins

Decide which item is the join path and refuse to let other items impersonate it. "Sign in" is for people who already have an account. "Apply," "List," or "Join as a carrier" is for people who do not. Mixing them trains the wrong click. A new host who hits a password field thinks they have already failed.

The join item should go to the same place from every page: a short form or a clear checklist, not a marketing page that asks them to choose a side again. If you need different forms for different services, the menu can expose those services by name. It should not expose your information architecture.

On pages meant for the second side, you may swap the emphasis. A campaign landing page for diners can lead with booking. The global header can stay stable. Stability is part of being understandable. A header that reorders itself by audience often reorders itself by bug, and regulars lose the path they memorized.

Check the path on a phone, in the condensed menu. The join item should be visible without a treasure hunt through nested drawers. If it sits under "More," it is not the path. Promote it. Demote a departmental page instead.

## Where proof and price live in the map

Pricing and proof are jobs. Give them labels a skeptic would click. "Fees" is often better than "Pricing" if that is the word in the market. "A night we ran" or "Recent loads" can be better than "Case studies," which sounds like a vendor. Pick one phrase and use it in the menu, the page title, and the first heading.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that describe the page and that are not a repeated block of boilerplate. Navigation and titles should agree. If the menu says "Fees" and the title says "Flexible partnership opportunities," you have two names for one page, and search results will inherit the confusion. Align them.

Do not hide proof only inside a blog no one is told about. If the case is part of the argument, it belongs in the map. A footer link titled "Learn" is where essays go to disappear. Name the story the way the scarce side would search for it.

Secondary pages, such as a privacy note or a payout schedule, can live in the footer. They still need plain labels. "Legal" as a single blob forces a person with a specific question to open a PDF they did not want. "Payout schedule" and "Privacy" can sit side by side.

## The footer is still navigation

Treat the footer as the long version of the map, not as a junk drawer. Group it by side when both sides use the site. Hosts: apply, fees, what we refuse, a story. Guests: book, how a night works. Shared: sign in, privacy, contact.

Repeat the join path once in the footer for the person who scrolled through a proof page and is ready. Same words. A second, vaguer call to action ("Let's build the future together") splits the click and sounds like a different company.

Include a way back to the homepage that is the logo, with an accessible name that is the company name. Do not make the logo the only way to reach "Apply." Logos are a convention for home. They are a poor convention for the action that pays the market.

Review the footer every time you add a campaign page. Campaigns breed one-off links. A footer that grows by accumulation stops being a map and becomes a history of the quarter.

## Check the map with five people

Sit with five people who match the side you need first. Do not explain the product first. Show the header on a phone and ask the three questions: how would you join, where is the fee, where is a real example. Note the words they use when they get lost. Those words are candidates for labels. The words you have to define are candidates for deletion.

Then run the same three questions with one person from the other side. You are checking that their door exists, not that the menu has become symmetrical. If they cannot find a way to book, add a plain item. If they can only find their way by taking the scarce side's button, you have a routing bug, and it will pollute your applicant pool.

Fix labels in a single pass across header, footer, buttons, and titles. A navigation change that updates the menu and forgets the button on the pricing page recreates the fork you just closed.

## Two products still share one map

Some markets split into two apps or two logged-in homes. The public site should not pretend to be both apps. It should route. The header sends a host to the host application and a guest to the guest booking flow, with labels that say so. Inside the product, navigation can be denser, because those people already know which side they are on.

Do not make the marketing menu a mirror of the app's settings. Settings are a job for members. Applicants do not need "Notifications" beside "Fees." If a member lands on the marketing site by habit, "Sign in" is their door. Keep it easy to see and hard to confuse with "Apply."

Write the map down in a single file the design and the build both use. Hanabi's sites are built in Next.js, and a header that is a shared component will stay honest only if the labels in that component are the labels in the copy doc. A one-off banner with a new verb undoes the map on the one page where you bought traffic.

The pictures have to tell the same story as the labels. A menu can say "a real dinner" while the photography still shows two abstract buttons and a mood. That gap is [photography direction for a two-sided marketplace](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-two-sided-marketplace).

If you want to sort the map before you redraw the header, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min).
